paras: The lynching of John Brown took place on August 4, 1890, near Anderson, Texas, when a crowd of citizens seized Brown, a Black prisoner accused of raping a white girl, from the keeping of Sheriff Scott and hanged him. According to the reports, his body was then filled with bullets, and the papers stated that he had confessed before he died. Besides Texas papers, a United Press dispatch carried the news to North Carolina, Virginia and Oregon.

Brown, described as "colored" and as "a negro," was accused of raping a white girl near Iola, an assault a Navasota dispatch placed "in this county." He had been held in the Houston jail for safe-keeping. The Fort Worth Gazette's Anderson correspondent did not name the girl, describing her only as "well connected and of good family."

The lynching fell on the same day as a courthouse mass meeting at Anderson, which the same correspondent said drew at least 1,500 people in a contest over the courthouse. Speakers there denounced men who would "run negroes from other counties to vote in our contest."

Brown was brought back from Houston to Anderson during the night of August 3 or early on the morning of August 4, and Sheriff Scott hid him in a private house. According to the Anderson letter, a crowd of 500 citizens demanded the prisoner, and when Scott refused to give him up they began a search and soon found him. He was carried two miles from town and hanged, with the correspondent putting the number present at "at least 2000 of our people." The Navasota special gave the time as about 3:50 p.m. and said the crowd "filled his carcass with bullets."

Both the special and the Anderson letter said Brown confessed. The correspondent wrote that Brown said "he was guilty and ought to die" and told the reporter he had watched for a chance to catch the girl for about three weeks, statements that rest only on the reporters at the scene. After the hanging, the letter said, the people went to their homes.

The district court adjourned for the term, and the county court continued all cases until the fall term "on account of so much excitement." No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage.

The Fort Worth Daily Gazette printed the first special from Navasota under the headline "A Rape Flend [Fiend] Lynched" and, a day later, the Anderson correspondence headed "The Anderson Lynching," whose subhead announced that "The Negro Made a Confession Before He was Strung up." The Anderson letter stated flatly that Brown "raped a white girl" and counted the crowd as "our people." On August 7 the Fort Worth Weekly Gazette reprinted that letter in a garbled text that named the victim "John Town" and gave the distance as "10 miles."

Outside Texas the story traveled as a brief United Press dispatch datelined Navasota, August 5. The Raleigh Daily State Chronicle ran it as "Judre Lynch Rampart" [Judge Lynch Rampant] and the Roanoke Times as "Lynched In Texas," while the Salem, Oregon, Evening Capital Journal folded it into a column of paragraphs, without Brown's name and with the place garbled as "Nova Sotia, Texas." The San Antonio Daily Light reduced it to one line of state news saying Brown was "strung up by the citizens of Navasota" for a crime "he confessed." None of these white papers questioned the charge or the confession or criticized the crowd, and no account of the lynching was found in the Black press.

The wire dispatch and the San Antonio brief tied the hanging to Navasota, while the Anderson correspondence placed it two miles from Anderson. Navasota appears to have been only the telegraph point, since the first special from there said "a report reached here from Anderson." The wire also said Brown was "taken from jail," whereas the original special and the Anderson letter, the local account, both said the sheriff had hidden him and the crowd found him by search.
